By CLAUDIA HESS and JAMES C. MCGRATH
A team of scientists has found a way to resurrect an extinct species by using DNA from its closest living relative — in this case, horses that still roam on Earth today.
In one experiment reported Tuesday at a meeting here of evolutionary biologists, researchers were able to create embryos with genetic material taken directly from mammoths’ cells preserved for more than 30 years inside frozen permafrost near Siberia’s Arctic coast.
They also used another technique called cloning: They took skin cell samples from two Asian elephants kept as pets in zoos in Japan and China; then they injected those into eggs removed from female African elephants who had been artificially inseminated but not fertilized.
Both techniques produced healthy elephant calves within weeks after birth last year, according to Drs. George M. Church and Keith A. Crandall of Harvard University, whose research was presented during a session devoted entirely to “de-extinction.”
Dr. Church said he hoped his work would help people understand how far science can go toward reviving lost creatures like woolly rhinos or saber-toothed tigers if it could be done safely without harming other animals.
“It may sound crazy,” he acknowledged, adding later, however, “I think we’re going down some very interesting roads.”

S3). This is an enormous undertaking; there are about three billion base pairs to be sequenced--about one million times more than was needed just five years ago when researchers first began sequencing individual genomes from bacteria such as E.coli. But this project will have far-reaching implications because we now know how our bodies work at their most basic level. We can begin looking into diseases like cancer with new eyes, since many cancers result not only from mutations but also from changes in gene expression caused by environmental factors. The process is similar in some ways to what's already being done with silicon-based panels: it involves depositing layers on top of each other using chemical vapor deposition techniques; but instead of starting from scratch like most manufacturers do today by melting down raw materials into ingots before slicing them up later, this one starts out as powder made through another kind of reaction between chemicals.
